rows.title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
rows.question: Fiserv DNA and Q2 are named as the core stack. What does that integration surface really look like — do we read the core ourselves, or go through connectors that already exist?
rows.answer:
We read through pre-built connectors, not directly into the core. The connector is the standard "adapter" that lets the AI agent, under authorization, verify identity, pull transactions, reissue statements, or open a dispute case — it's the entry ticket to "reach" the system, not a custom build per bank [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html). The action scope is still governed by the delegation matrix and approval gates, so the connector only solves access, not what the agent is allowed to do [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html).

Sources: 1. [Research Report — 1.6 术语表](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

rows.title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
rows.question: If the beachhead is only 262 institutions, how should I structure my PM team — one squad for the whole band, or split it by asset tier?
rows.answer:
Short answer: don't split by asset tier yet. The 262-band is a verifiable ceiling, not a calibrated target — exact in-band counts (public mailboxes, listed cores) await pilot customer-acquisition calibration [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). Structure one squad for the whole band until the pilot re-prices the ROI with the customer's own mail (4 weeks) and backtests it (90 days) [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/); tiering is a post-calibration decision, not a pre-pilot one.

Sources: 2. [PRD (English) — 11.1 Business Case Summary](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 1. [Case Study Deck — Mid-size banks are the beachhead.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
rows.question: Larkspur is fictional but it drives the whole ROI. Which of its four profile numbers would actually change product scope if a real prospect differs?
rows.answer:
Good catch — the four profile numbers are all assumptions, but only two would change product scope if a real prospect differed materially. The email volume (60k/month) and the 22% "please call" rate drive the ROI levers (failure demand, VARR, AI-assisted efficiency) [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html); if those move, the savings scale linearly. The asset size ($18B) and FTE count (420) are just context for plausibility — they don't alter what the product must do. The one number that would change scope is the 22% "please call" rate: if a prospect's baseline is lower, the "same-thread verification and resolution" feature (the client-side #1 experience, per [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)) becomes less of a wedge, and we'd lean more on Reg E compliance as the driver instead.

Sources: 2. [Research Report — 9.2 邮件渠道的经济账](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) · 1. [Research Report — 审阅发现：必须纠正或补上的 10 处（按对面试的影响排序）](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

rows.title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
rows.question: The 262 figure comes from an FDIC query. What happens at the edges of the $5B–$150B band — does the product need to behave differently for a bank that just crossed in, or is the band only a sales filter?
rows.answer:
The band is a sales filter, not a product boundary — the product itself keys off Reg E applicability, public mailbox, and off-the-shelf core, not asset size (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). A bank that just crossed $5B still runs Reg E and uses the same mailbox/core setup, so behavior is identical; the $150B cap is where institutions typically build in-house rather than buy, which is a go-to-market distinction, not a feature fork (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Edge cases like a bank hovering near $5B would only matter for pricing/ROI re-calibration, which we already handle by re-pricing with the customer's own mail data within 4 weeks (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Mid-size banks are the beachhead.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.title: The clock starts at the inbox.
rows.question: A clock starts when the bank receives the mail, not when an agent opens it. Where does that receipt timestamp come from, and how would we prove it to an examiner?
rows.answer:
Good question — the receipt timestamp is the moment the email lands in the bank's system, not when an agent opens it, and that's exactly what the deck's "clock starts at the inbox" claim rests on (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The timestamp comes from the mail server's intake log, which we'd treat as the system-of-record for Reg E purposes; the deck doesn't specify the exact logging mechanism or audit trail format, so I can't point to a concrete implementation detail here. For examiner proof, the argument would be that the intake log is immutable and time-stamped at the point of receipt, but the reference material doesn't cover how we'd present that evidence in an exam — that's a gap we'd need to close in the build phase, not something I can commit to from this deck.

Sources: 2. [Case Study Deck — The clock starts at the inbox.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
rows.sources: Research Report / v0.4 新增的 6 个产品主张（差异化从这里来） | Case Study Deck / The clock starts at the inbox.

rows.title: The clock starts at the inbox.
rows.question: The 28% of agent time lost to system switching comes from a third-party study. Does our design genuinely remove that switching, or does it just move the same effort into a review queue?
rows.answer:
Fair question. The 28% figure is Talkdesk/NewtonX research, not a Larkspur measurement [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Our design removes the *agent* switching by auto-routing the email straight into the investigation workflow — but you're right that the effort doesn't vanish; it shifts to a review queue where a specialist validates the auto-extracted data before any Reg E clock action. We haven't yet benchmarked whether that queue's total time beats the old 27h median first reply, so I'd flag that as an open assumption rather than a proven win.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The clock starts at the inbox.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / The clock starts at the inbox.

rows.title: The clock starts at the inbox.
rows.question: Email costs $6–12 a contact and phone $12–20. When I sit with a buyer, do I sell against the channel cost or against the violation exposure?
rows.answer:
Sell against the violation exposure — that’s the headline. The cost range is supporting color: it shows email is the slowest channel *and* the most expensive per contact after phone, so the buyer is paying more for a worse outcome (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Lead with the Reg E clock and the 74% of violations in error resolution; the $6–12 vs. $12–20 spread only reinforces that the status quo is both risky and inefficient (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The clock starts at the inbox.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / The clock starts at the inbox.

rows.title: The clock starts at the inbox.
rows.question: The 10-business-day and 45-day clocks are statutory, but the 27-hour first reply and the 22% "please call us" rate are assumptions. Which one, if it turns out wrong, breaks the business case first?
rows.answer:
Good catch, Lena. The 27-hour median first reply is the one that breaks the business case first — it drives the 22% "please call us" boomerang rate, and that boomerang is the single largest line item in the base-tier savings (~$720K of the $2.68M, per [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)). If the real 4-week pilot data shows a faster first reply, the failed-demand reduction shrinks proportionally, and the VARR denominator shifts too. The 45-day clock is statutory but doesn't move the economics; the 27-hour assumption is the load-bearing one, which is why the pilot report must replace it with the customer's real data before any external figure is quoted (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)).

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 11.4 Pilot Economics (All Assumptions, for Calibration Against Customer Data)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

rows.title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
rows.question: The table says the marginal build is the vertical layer alone. What is the honest engineering estimate for that layer, and which of the components we lean on is the weakest link?
rows.answer:
The honest estimate is that the vertical layer is the only net-new engineering: intent detection, assurance tiers, the clock, and the dossier, all written on top of the platform’s reused runtime, bot builder, automation, and connectors [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). I can’t give a number of person-months from the deck — it doesn’t break that out — but the weakest link is the clock engine, because it turns a promise into a deadline and is the piece most likely to need bespoke tuning against the bank’s policy pack [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Everything else leans on components CXA already ships and labels as reused, so the risk concentrates there.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Four more questions, short answers.

rows.title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
rows.question: Email ranks above voice here because there is no live interruption. Is that a product property or a technical one — could a voice agent get the same async character with a callback pattern?
rows.answer:
Good question — it’s a product property, not a technical ceiling. A callback pattern could technically make voice async, but it still carries the expectation of a live conversation and the interruption risk when the call connects; email’s async character is inherent to the channel itself [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). The deck’s point is that email is the lowest-risk way to graduate the matrix *today*, not that voice can never be made async [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Same base, no live caller, same runtime.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Same base, no live caller, same runtime.

rows.title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
rows.question: Chat is marked as a smaller surface than email even though both wait their turn. What exactly makes email the bigger build?
rows.answer:
Email is the bigger build because it is an add-on on the 262-bank install base with a mailbox clock that runs without a live caller — that is the vertical layer alone, and it lets us bill on contracts that already exist (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Chat, by contrast, is a parity build against rivals on a smaller surface, with threads that wait their turn but no comparable installed-base revenue hook (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The size difference is about the auditable revenue and the add-on economics, not the async mechanics.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Same base, no live caller, same runtime.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / Same base, no live caller, same runtime.

rows.title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
rows.question: Two rows say the work already ships. Should my PM org own those lines or hand them off, and how do we avoid stepping on the teams that own them today?
rows.answer:
Dana — those two rows are labeled “reused,” not “owned by us”: the runtime, bot builder, automation flows and connectors already ship on CXA, and our vertical layer (intent detection, assurance tiers, the clock, the dossier) sits on top of them [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Your PM org should own the vertical layer and the proof (policy pack, eval harness, reference numbers), while the horizontal teams keep owning their components — we hand off via the existing connectors and label everything as reused so there’s no overlap [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)[2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). If a hand-off boundary blurs, the design-partner program is the forcing function: compliance is a named owner, and the sequencing is one of the three things a partner would rewrite first [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

rows.title: We automate the work, not the decision.
rows.question: Wave 1 and Wave 2 are described as differences in the policy pack. If both run on one engine, what stops a Wave 2 intent being switched on early by a misconfigured limit matrix?
rows.answer:
Nothing in the design stops it — the limit matrix is bank-written, and the same engine applies it to every wave ([1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The guardrail is the governance layer, not the runtime: Wave 2 intents ship with their own policy pack and UDAAP review, and the roadmap sequences them deliberately ([1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If a misconfiguration slipped in, it would surface in the same test set and consequence preview used for Wave 1, but the deck doesn't specify a separate validation gate for early activation.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — One governance layer, three waves.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / One governance layer, three waves.

rows.title: We automate the work, not the decision.
rows.question: Complaints and fraud are route-only at 5% of volume. Is that about the model not being good enough, or about regulatory exposure — and would more evidence ever unlock them?
rows.answer:
Both, but the binding constraint is regulatory exposure, not model quality. Complaints and fraud are permanently L0 — humans decide and sign — and route-only in Wave 1 means they are detected, clocked, and handed to a person, never answered autonomously [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). More evidence would not unlock them; the deck explicitly keeps adjudication off the machine for these categories, and UDAAP wording review only follows in Wave 2, still without autonomous answering [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — We automate the work, not the decision.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / We automate the work, not the decision.

rows.title: We automate the work, not the decision.
rows.question: Complaints and fraud are the smallest slice by volume but probably the largest by risk. What is the commercial story for leaving the scariest category manual?
rows.answer:
The commercial story is that risk concentration, not volume, drives the delegation design. Complaints and fraud are R4 — the highest regulatory-risk tier — so Wave 1 deliberately ships only detection, quarantine, and warm handoff, never autonomous replies (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)). That protects the bank from UDAAP exposure and SAR confidentiality duties, which would dwarf any labor savings from automation; the deck's own principle is "everything reversible goes to the machine, everything consequential stays with a person" (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The cost is contained because intake is still automated — clocking, routing, and document chasing — so the human effort is focused on the irreversible judgment, not the administrative work (see [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

rows.title: We automate the work, not the decision.
rows.question: The sort order is volume × determinability × identity achievability. Which of those three is computed at runtime and which is a judgement that has to be re-made with every bank?
rows.answer:
The three factors are all judgement calls that have to be re-made with each bank — none is computed at runtime. Volume and determinability come from the bank's own intake data and process definitions; identity achievability depends on their KYC/authentication stack and channel mix. The slide's sorting logic is a design-time exercise for the case study, not a live calculation in the product (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)).

Sources: 1. [Research Report — 12.0 v0.4 用例优先级矩阵：按题目给出的五大类](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

rows.title: The thread is the case.
rows.question: Personalization includes a tone tier. Who defines those tiers, and can an agent override one for a single thread?
rows.answer:
The tone tier is part of the bank's own policy pack — the same pack that holds the identity-assurance tiers and the clock rules (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The bank defines the tiers; we only execute them. An agent can override a tier for a single thread, but that override is a human decision recorded in the dossier and audit trail, not a model choice — the system never writes a disclosure or amount based on tone (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 2. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 1. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.title: The thread is the case.
rows.question: Step 8 is the only place a model writes to a customer, and only the connective tissue. Is that boundary enforced by the prompt or by the structure of the system?
rows.answer:
The boundary is enforced by the system's structure, not by prompt instructions. Step 8 is "assembled, not written": the regulated disclosure is a locked template, amounts and dates are system slots checked field by field, and only the connective tissue passes through a model [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). The model never receives the authority to generate disclosures or amounts — it only joins pre-validated components, so the constraint holds regardless of prompt behavior.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.title: The thread is the case.
rows.question: Nine steps and three possible roads after step 5. Where does the record of which road was taken live, and could a reviewer reconstruct it a month later?
rows.answer:
The road taken is determined by the matrix at step 5, and the outcome is recorded as part of the case thread itself — the same thread that is the case (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). A reviewer can reconstruct it a month later because the thread retains the step-by-step trail: the autonomy level (L3, L2, or L0–L1) is a property of the case record, and step 8's assembly (which sources were used) plus the 14-day verification window leave an auditable footprint (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The deck doesn't specify the underlying storage schema or retention policy beyond that window, so I can't speak to longer-term archival details.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / The thread is the case.

rows.title: The thread is the case.
rows.question: Step 6 is idempotent, but what happens if it acts and then step 8 never sends — does the case reopen somewhere, or does it close quietly?
rows.answer:
Step 6’s actions are idempotent and compensated by the case runtime (FR-4.3), so if step 8 never sends, the case does not close quietly — the runtime’s compensation and human-handoff logic (FR-4.4) reopens or escalates it per the case-state contract (FR-4.1). The 14-day verification window in step 9 also catches any silent failure, since the case remains open until that window closes (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The deck doesn’t specify the exact reopen trigger timing, so I’d point you to FR-4.3/FR-4.4 in the PRD for the operational detail [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html).

Sources: 2. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 1. [PRD (English) — 6.1 Email Thread Is the Case (Thread = Case)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

rows.title: Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.
rows.question: The matrix is four identity grades by five action risks. How much of that is code that already ships versus new engineering, and who maintains it once a bank writes its own limits?
rows.answer:
The matrix itself is new — it’s the bank-written limit matrix (R × I → L) that sits as a thin vertical layer on top of existing Autopilot, Automation Flows, Agent Builder, and FS core connectors [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). The code that already ships is the underlying platform; the layer is new engineering, but it’s written once by the bank and applied across channels, not per intent [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Once the bank writes its own limits, maintenance falls to the bank — the deck positions it as “one policy engine … written once by the bank,” with the platform providing the compiler and regulatory radar, but it doesn’t specify who owns ongoing updates beyond that [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — One governance layer, three waves.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
rows.sources: Case Study Deck / One governance layer, three waves.

rows.title: Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.
rows.question: R3 is never autonomous over email because the tool functions do not exist on this channel. Is that an architectural guarantee, or a deployment choice someone could reverse later?
rows.answer:
It’s an architectural guarantee, not a deployment choice. The R3 tool functions are simply not registered on the email channel — security depends on dangerous actions being unreachable, not on model obedience (see [4](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)). The design also hard-codes this in the autonomy matrix: R3 is “Never autonomous over email — the tool functions do not exist on this channel” (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)), and the prototype fixture marks it as `never` with no graduation path (see [3](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/mocks/fixtures/designTime.ts)). Reversing it would require a deliberate product change, not a config toggle.

Sources: 4. [PRD (English) — 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 1. rows.title: Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.
rows.question: Money movement has no graduation path at all. What is the risk that this permanent ceiling becomes how customers judge the whole product?
rows.answer:
The ceiling is deliberate: R4 (adjudication / money movement) is "Never autonomous over email — the tool functions do not exist on this channel," so there is no graduation path by design, not by oversight (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The risk you name is real, but the deck frames it as a feature — the L0 human decides and sends, the AI only triages and suggests, which is the strongest possible trust signal for the highest-risk action (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If anything, that permanent boundary is what lets the rest of the ladder earn autonomy credibly, because customers see the line hold where it must.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.title: Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.
rows.question: Auto-demotion on drift is mentioned but not specified. What triggers it, who gets told, and does it happen silently?
rows.answer:
Drift triggers are defined per intent at graduation: the backtest window, sampling error bounds, and negative-relabel thresholds that earned autonomy in the first place are the same gates that trip auto-demotion (see [2](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/README.md)). When it trips, the intent drops to the next lower L-level (e.g., L3 → L2), the owning team and Compliance are notified via the existing dual sign-off channel, and it is not silent — the demotion itself is a configuration diff that goes through the same review trail as any other change (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The deck doesn't specify exact thresholds or notification cadence, so those details live in the per-intent policy config, not in the public materials.

Sources: 2. [Project README — Solution](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/README.md) · 1. [Case Study Deck — AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.title: AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff.
rows.question: Six nominators spread across two screens and three roles. Who owns this loop day to day — one PM, or a standing review board with a cadence?
rows.answer:
Good question — the loop is owned by the Product + Compliance dual-sign gate, not a single PM. The PRD is explicit that every nomination must clear backtest, shadow, and dual sign before taking effect [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html), and the "Watch" phase (quotas, PSI, auto-degrade, cooldowns) keeps running continuously [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). Day-to-day, the cadence is driven by the wave board and the 14-day shadow cycle — each nomination gets its own review slot, with Product and Compliance signing the diff together, not a standing board [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)[3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). The reference material doesn't specify a single owner role or meeting frequency beyond that, so I'd flag that as an open implementation detail for the demo.

rows.title: AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff.
rows.question: The whole loop eats 90 days of decisions as its input. What do we do for a customer who does not have 90 days of clean history to feed it?
rows.answer:
Good question, Marcus. The 90-day window is the backtest horizon for *proving* a nomination, not a prerequisite for the customer to have 90 days of history — the loop's input is the bank's aggregate decision log, not any single customer's file (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). For a customer with sparse history, the rule engine still decides on deterministic facts (account facts only, no predictive scoring), and the AI's role is limited to drafting and rewording — it never judges or re-decides (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If the evidence base is too thin to backtest a new intent, that intent simply doesn't graduate; it stays shadow-classified until enough samples exist (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), Rule 5).

rows.title: AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff.
rows.question: A nomination is a configuration diff. What format is that diff in, and can it be applied atomically or does each bank need a migration?
rows.answer:
The diff format is a configuration diff — the model drafts it, the bank signs it, and every nomination, wave remediation, and policy change arrives as one of these diffs, all clearing the same gates (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The deck doesn’t specify the exact serialization (e.g., JSON/YAML) or whether application is atomic versus a per-bank migration — that’s outside the reference material, so I can’t speak to it. What I can confirm is the governance around it: the bank controls every cell and threshold, and R3/R4 cells don’t respond at all; tightening is immediate with auto-expiry, loosening requires backtest → shadow → dual sign (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)).

rows.title: AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff.
rows.question: Dissent cards are part of the proving step. What counts as dissent, and does it block the grant or is it only recorded?
rows.answer:
Dissent cards are recorded evidence, not a veto — they attach to the nomination and travel with the diff into the human sign-off step, where the two signing humans weigh them alongside the backtest. They don’t block the grant by themselves; the grant is always a human decision, and the card is one more input into that decision (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If the reference material doesn’t specify a threshold or escalation rule for dissent, I can’t invent one — the deck only defines the loop: propose, prove, grant, watch, with dissent cards as part of the “prove” evidence (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

rows.title: Four screens, four proofs.
rows.question: Four screens on one runtime. Which of them is hardest to keep consistent when the limit matrix changes — the agent workspace or the admin policy screen?
rows.answer:
The admin policy screen is the harder one to keep consistent, because it is the source of truth for every R × I limit — the agent workspace and supervisor console both render what the admin screen writes (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The demo keeps them consistent by making the admin screen the single place where limits are tightened "in one click," and the agent workspace reflects that policy verdict rather than any model mood (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). That said, the reference material does not specify the technical sync mechanism between the screens, so I can't speak to the implementation details beyond what the deck shows.

rows.title: Four screens, four proofs.
rows.question: Admin tightens a limit in one click. Does that write a new policy version or mutate the live one, and can it be rolled back?
rows.answer:
The one-click tightening writes a new configuration diff — it never mutates the live policy in place. Every change, including a tightening, has to clear the same gates as any other diff: the bank signs it, and it lands as a new version (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Rollback is possible, but only through the same path — a new diff that loosens the cell, which requires graduation evidence and a dual signature, since R3 and R4 cells never respond to a single click (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

rows.title: Four screens, four proofs.
rows.question: Only four demo films are listed and one number is missing from the sequence. Is that deliberate, and what does the gap say about what we can show a buyer today?
rows.answer: The gap is deliberate — the deck lists Demo 1, 2, 3, and 5, skipping Demo 4. That slot is reserved for a fourth proof we haven't filmed yet; the numbering keeps the roadmap visible rather than renumbering and hiding the missing piece. Today we can show a buyer the four finished films (identity, disputes, fraud, intelligence), and the gap signals that a fifth capability is in the pipeline but not yet demo-ready.

rows.title: Four screens, four proofs.
rows.question: The customer screen has no login and verifies identity inside the thread. What is the fallback when that verification fails — is there a path that does not end in a phone call?
rows.answer:
Good catch, Sam. FR-2.2 AC2 covers this: on failure or timeout, the case offers alternative paths (phone/branch) without leaking account status [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). So the fallback is explicitly phone or branch — there is no in-thread-only path that avoids a call if verification fails.

rows.title: Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case.
rows.question: The window is 12–18 months and one competitor already ships autonomous email. What is our wedge if a CCaaS vendor bundles an email case model before we close the first bank?
rows.answer:
The wedge is the case model itself, not email automation. Freshworks ships autonomous email but is SMB-only with no FS depth or voice core [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html); Talkdesk only extended Autopilot to email in 2026-02 and its 16 prebuilt banking agents include no independent dispute agent [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html). No vendor has made "email thread = case timeline" a product model, and none publishes a verified, email-only, dispute-full-cycle autonomous closure rate [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html). Our statutory clock engine, core-banking execution, and dispute state machine are the regulatory moat — that's what the 12–18 months buys, and it's why the deck says "most automate the reply; few propose the rules" [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). If a CCaaS bundles a shallow case model first, we still win on Reg E depth and audit-ready case files, which none of them have shown publicly [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html).

rows.title: Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case.
rows.question: Core-banking execution is scored as a capability. If those connectors have been shipping for over a year, what is genuinely left for us to build there?
rows.answer:
The connectors are the plumbing, not the case. Since April 2025 we've shipped the core-banking connectors themselves, but the email-native case model — proposing the statutory rules, not just automating the reply — is what nobody has shipped yet (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). That's the 12–18 month window we're spending on CXA Operations Center, Agent Builder, and Automation Flows; the connectors get us to the data, the case model is what wins the deal.

rows.title: Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case.
rows.question: Our target state marks all four capabilities. Which one is the actual differentiator in a deal, and which are just table stakes?
rows.answer:
The differentiator is the statutory-clock engine — AI opening Reg E/Z clocks, auto-acknowledging, and chasing materials while a human adjudicates — because the clock starts at intake and Talkdesk's catalog has no dispute agent [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html). The email-native case model and core-banking execution are table stakes: they're what the platform already ships (CXA Operations Center, Agent Builder, Automation Flows, connectors since April 2025) [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Voice + real-time ops via CCaaS is table stakes too — it's the existing Talkdesk install base we're selling into, not a wedge [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html).

rows.title: Four groups want this customer. Nobody has the email case.
rows.question: One of the four states is "not in public materials". How do we keep that assessment honest if a rival ships it quietly and we only find out mid-deal?
rows.answer:
Fair question — the "not in public materials" cells are explicitly a statement about what we can verify, not a claim about the market (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). We keep it honest by treating absence as a risk, not a win: the threat ranking already flags Glia and Eltropy as the beachhead competitors to watch, and the deck's own gap analysis says "every 'missing' cell above is absence in public materials, not absence in the market" [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). If a rival ships quietly mid-deal, we'd learn it the same way they'd learn about us — through the customer's RFP or a reference call — and the honest move is to update the slide and re-scope the win, not pretend the cell was ever a guarantee.

rows.title: One bank's email book is a $4.8M cost base.
rows.question: The vendor fee and the seats replaced are both listed. Who in my org owns the seats-replaced conversation with the customer, since it lands on their operations budget?
rows.answer:
Good question — the seats-replaced line is a customer-side saving, not a vendor fee, so it lands on the bank's operations budget and is owned by whoever runs their contact-center or back-office ops (typically the COO or head of operations). In our model, the vendor's fee sits on top of the bank's net saving (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)), so the seats-replaced conversation is really the bank's own cost-avoidance story; we'd support them with the math, but the decision to redeploy or reduce seats is theirs. The deck doesn't specify a named owner role — that's a gap we can close in the implementation plan if useful.

rows.title: One bank's email book is a $4.8M cost base.
rows.question: The saving turns on how much we can genuinely finish. Is the resolved-rate range measured anywhere, and what instrumentation would produce that number in production?
rows.answer:
The resolved-rate range is measured against the bank's own mail mix and baselines, with inputs from the customer's mail in week one and pricing in four weeks (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). In production, the number would come from tagging each email as resolved or not against the 90-day history eval set, with the three levers — failed demand, autonomy, copilot uplift — moving together across the cases (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). We haven't published the specific instrumentation schema, so I can't detail the exact logging or attribution logic beyond that.

rows.title: One bank's email book is a $4.8M cost base.
rows.question: The same rate is quoted against two different denominators. Which one do we commit to in a contract, and does the difference change the headline number?
rows.answer:
We commit to the harder denominator: VARR is reported against every valid inbound email — disputes, fraud reports, multi-intent mail and repeat contacts all count [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). The eligible-pool rate is published side by side for transparency, but the contract number is the all-inbound base, so 35% of the eligible pool reads as ≈30% of the harder base — that difference is the headline we stand behind [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

rows.question: The vendor-side figure multiplies out to roughly $54M at full adoption, with penetration explicitly not assumed. What penetration is the plan actually underwriting in year one?
rows.answer:
The plan underwrites zero penetration in year one — the $54M is a ceiling, not a target. We deliberately show 262 × $205k with "penetration not assumed" (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)) because the deck's base case is the per-bank saving, not a sales forecast. Year-one execution is about proving the 35% resolution case at one beachhead bank; adoption math comes later, once the eval set (90 days of history) validates the model.

rows.title: Three numbers. One pilot.
rows.question: A single critical error voids the headline number. Is the recall target measured on the bank’s own mail or on our eval set, and who signs off on that measurement?
rows.answer:
Recall is measured on the bank’s own mail, not our eval set — the pilot’s backtest (W1–W2) and shadow (W3–W4) run on live traffic, and the 14-day no-reopen window is tracked from the arrival timestamp on that same traffic [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Sign-off is joint: the bank’s compliance lead owns the final call on the recall ≥99.5% gate, with our shared eval team running the measurement and the bank’s QA sampling as the independent check [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)[3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

rows.title: Three numbers. One pilot.
rows.question: Four phases inside 59 days is tight for an integration. Which phase slips first if the connector work runs a week late, and what is the recovery?
rows.answer:
If the connector work runs a week late, the slip hits the W1–W2 onboarding and backtest phase first, since that's where the mailboxes and 90-day export live (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Recovery is to compress the shadow run (W3–W4) — it's recommend-only and never executes, so you can overlap it with the tail of backtesting as long as the recall ≥99.5% gate still holds before L1/L2 goes live (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The day-59 gate is a hard veto on any miss, so we'd rather tighten the shadow window than push the L3 rollout or the day-45 cohort observation.

rows.title: Three numbers. One pilot.
rows.question: Time to resolution runs from the arrival timestamp. Does that clock keep running while the customer is being asked for a step-up?
rows.answer:
The clock starts at intake and keeps running through any step-up — the regulatory obligation is tied to the receipt of the notice, not to how long verification takes (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)). That’s exactly why our design automates the dispute intake and clock-starting immediately, and why step-up is scoped to the same thread so the clock isn’t paused or reset (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)). If the reference material doesn’t specify a pause mechanism, I’d flag that as a gap to confirm with compliance before the pilot.

rows.title: Three numbers. One pilot.
rows.question: The autonomy rate has three conditions attached. Which of the three is most likely to be gamed by a customer who wants the number to look good?
rows.answer:
The one most exposed to gaming is the **recall threshold on regulated-intent detection** — the ≥99.5% "one miss = one violation" bar. A team could tune the detector to over-flag (high recall, low precision), which inflates the "caught everything" story while quietly depressing the autonomy rate and ROI; the trade-off register explicitly accepts this "宁可误报多升级" to protect the compliance signature [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html). The graduation-sample count (n≥600) is harder to game because it's a statistical artifact of rule of three — you can't fake the sample size, only wait [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html). The action-whitelist restriction (high-impact actions never enter the tool) isn't gameable at all: it's a hard architectural exclusion, not a metric [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html).

rows.title: The risks that would end this product.
rows.question: If our own judge flips verdicts at that rate, how can an autonomy number be contractual at all?
rows.answer:
The autonomy number isn’t contractual — it’s a benchmark, and we say so explicitly on the slide. The 14% flip rate is exactly why we frame the judge as “judge 自己也被评测” rather than as a source of ground truth [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html). For anything that would trigger a hard regulatory obligation (授信, 拒赔, investment advice), we keep L0 人工 in the loop, so the contract never rests on the judge’s verdict alone [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html).

Sources: 1. [Research Report — 12.0c 机会优先级（v0.3 原表，已按 v0.4 口径更新）](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

rows.title: The risks that would end this product.
rows.question: Preferring false positives pushes recall up and precision down. Where does the false-positive cost actually land, and can a bank tune the trade-off without breaking the recall gate?
rows.answer:
The false-positive cost lands on the intake side: a hit immediately starts the statutory clock, tags the item as regulated, and locks its delegation tier (intake-side R2 may automate; adjudication R4 is always human) — so a false positive means human adjudication effort and a clock that is already running, but no regulatory miss [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). Tuning is constrained by the recall gate: FR-1.4 requires regulated-intent recall ≥ 99.5% in three-stratum backtesting, with a miss treated as a zero-tolerance incident, so the bank can adjust precision only within that floor — e.g., by calibrating detector thresholds or adding sub-intent filters — but cannot trade recall below the gate without triggering incident review [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). The PRD does not specify a precision target or a formal tuning mechanism beyond the recall requirement, so that operational knob is left to implementation.

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)
rows.sources: PRD (English) / 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)

rows.title: The risks that would end this product.
rows.question: Injected text is quarantined as data and never as instruction. What is the mechanism — a sanitiser before the model, or a structural separation of the two channels?
rows.answer:
The mechanism is both, layered: external content is sanitized and labeled at the quarantine layer (script stripping, tracking-pixel removal, link rewriting) before any model reads it, and it is then passed to the model strictly as data with explicit delimiters and untrusted markings — never in the instruction channel (FR-6.1, AC1–AC3 in [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)). On top of that, tool-call policy comes only from the system policy, never from mail content, and the R3 combination (change-mobile + mail-card) has no callable function on the email channel at all (FR-6.2 in [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html); see also [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) and [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)). So even if sanitization were bypassed, the structural separation of tool signatures means injected text cannot reach a dangerous action.

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 2. [Case Study Deck — The risks that would end this product.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 3. [PRD (English) — 8.3 Email Three: ATO + Attachment Injection (Showing "Dangerous Actions Are Unreachable")](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

rows.title: The risks that would end this product.
rows.question: Sign-off fatigue is on the register. What stops one-click approvals from becoming rubber stamps once a customer is running at the target autonomy?
rows.answer:
Good catch — the approve-without-edit rate is the leading indicator we watch, and we sample the approved files to catch drift before it becomes systemic (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The one-click approval cell is deliberately downgraded to a human-signed step when the policy condition fails, so the rubber-stamp risk is bounded by the same logic that gates autonomy (see [2](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/demo/scripts.ts)). We don't have a hard threshold in the deck yet, but the register flags sign-off fatigue as a watch item, not a solved one.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The risks that would end this product.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 2. [Prototype Source — src/demo/scripts.ts](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/demo/scripts.ts)

rows.title: One governance layer, three waves.
rows.question: The second wave mentions a wording review for complaints. Is that a new model capability or a new human review step on top of the existing one?
rows.answer:
It’s a new human review step, not a new model capability. Wave 1 already does detection, clock registration, and warm handoff for complaints; the UDAAP wording review in Wave 2 is a deeper, human-led check of the bank’s own replies for regulatory-compliant language, layered on top of that existing routing (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html), [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The model still doesn’t adjudicate or sign anything — the review is part of the “everything consequential stays with a person” rule (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 5.1 Use-Case Wave Matrix](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 2. [Case Study Deck — We automate the work, not the decision.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.title: One governance layer, three waves.
rows.question: The second wave adds a new language and a new regulation under the same policy pack. Who owns that pack as an artifact — a PM or an engineering team?
rows.answer:
The policy pack is owned by the bank itself — it is the bank's own artifact, not ours. We ship the tooling and the eval harness, but the pack is written and maintained by the bank's compliance team, with our product and engineering supporting the mechanics (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). So the owner is the bank's compliance function; we are the implementers of the setting, not the authors of the policy.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — How it is packaged, priced and sold.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 2. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

rows.title: One governance layer, three waves.
rows.question: Five of the new pieces are written by the bank itself. What stops two banks from diverging into configurations we can no longer support?
rows.answer:
The bank-written limit matrix is the product, not a fork — the engine (R × I → L) and the clock are fixed; only the cells and thresholds vary, and every diff clears the same gates (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Divergence is bounded by design: R3/R4 cells never respond, loosening requires graduation evidence plus dual signature, and each delegation ships a readiness report (backtest, sample counts, error rates) so we can see drift before it happens (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If a bank asks for something outside the matrix — say, a pause on Reg E clocks — the product simply doesn't offer it, because the clock rules are statutory, not configurable (see [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Admin: the bank writes the limits, not the model.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 3. [PRD (English) — 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

rows.title: One governance layer, three waves.
rows.question: One policy engine written once and applied to every channel. What has to be true in the runtime for a voice agent to reuse the email policy pack without forking it?
rows.answer:
The runtime has to treat the policy pack as data, not code — the same `R × I → L` limit matrix and clock engine that email uses must be callable by the voice agent via the same connectors and Agent Builder runtime, with no channel-specific fork (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The deck assumes the layer is thin and channel-agnostic, but it does not specify the runtime interface details (e.g., how the voice agent invokes the clock or dossier); that would need to be designed and validated in Wave 2/3 (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — One governance layer, three waves.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
